implementation_notes: `threading.local()` gives each thread a private attribute namespace: create one instance at module level and every thread that stores attributes on it sees only its own values, which is the standard carrier for per-thread state (the GIL does not make shared mutable state safe, it only serializes bytecode). Stack confinement needs no library at all - locals that never escape are thread-safe by construction. Keep this thread-scoped form when the state is genuinely bound to OS threads (for example a non-thread-safe C-extension handle or a per-worker connection), and switch to the contextvars variant whenever the unit of work is an asyncio task or coroutine, where threading.local state bleeds between concurrent tasks sharing one event-loop thread.
pitfalls: threading.local values are never cleaned up specially: long-lived worker threads keep them forever, and pooled workers carry per-request state into unrelated tasks if nothing resets it.
Storing a mutable object on a local attribute is still a race if that object itself is shared across threads - the attribute is per-thread, the object is not.
State stored under a local inside a coroutine running on an event-loop thread leaks to every other task scheduled on that thread.

variants.name: contextvars.ContextVar (task-scoped, PEP 567)
variants.implementation_notes: ContextVar values live in the current Context, and asyncio gives every Task its own context copied at creation time, so concurrent tasks on one event-loop thread no longer overwrite each other's state - the exact failure the contextvars documentation attributes to threading.local in concurrent code. `set()` affects the current context only and is undone by `reset(token)` or by leaving a `Context.run` scope; an unset variable raises LookupError unless a default is declared. Use ContextVar for anything that follows a request or operation; keep threading.local only for genuinely thread-bound resources.
variants.code_sketch:
import contextvars
tenant = contextvars.ContextVar("tenant")      # create at module level

async def handle(req):
    tenant.set(req.tenant)                       # this Task's context only
    await audit()                                # audit sees req.tenant
# cross a boundary explicitly: contextvars.copy_context().run(...)
pitfalls: Creating a ContextVar inside a closure/function ties it to contexts that hold strong references, preventing collection (documented: declare them at module level).

A callable scheduled on a loop or executor runs in the caller's context by default; state set inside the worker does not propagate back and may leak to unrelated callbacks unless copy_context() is used deliberately.
A shared mutable default undermines isolation: every context starts with the same object unless each task sets its own value.
